role: Creator & Curator — Prague, Czech Republic — Age 15
bio_paragraphs: I am a high school student in Prague with a self-directed research interest in mTOR signaling, longevity biology, and evidence-based science curation. I built Oliver's mTOR Atlas myself, with help from AI along the way, to create the kind of resource I wished existed when I began reading primary literature on the pathway: one structured database that holds studies, mechanisms, interventions, and honest evidence grades side by side, rather than scattered across dozens of review articles and pathway maps.

My current focus is mTOR regulation under dynamic rather than steady-state conditions — most of the literature treats mTORC1/mTORC2 activity as fixed rather than something that shifts over time in a real cell. I am interested in whether the pattern of activity over time — not just its average level — is what actually shapes outcomes like autophagy or growth. See {{RESEARCH_FOCUS_LINK}} in About for the frontier questions and studies behind it.
research_focus_intro: My current focus is mTOR regulation under dynamic rather than steady-state conditions. Most of the literature treats mTORC1/mTORC2 activity as fixed — a level, measured once, usually right after a nutrient jolt in a dish. Real cells never see a jolt like that: they see meals, exercise, sleep and waking, a rhythm underneath everything else.

I am interested in whether the pattern of activity over time — not just its average level — is what actually shapes outcomes like autophagy or growth. If it is, a lot of the field's single-time-point measurements are answering a different question than the one being asked. This section collects the frontier questions this raises, the studies that motivate them, and what is currently running or newly published that bears on them.
frontier_questions_intro: Five open framing questions in the Atlas grow directly out of this — not gaps in what has been measured, but questions about whether the standard way of measuring mTOR is even asking the right thing:

frontier_questions.title: Does mTORC1 carry information in the pattern of its activity over time, not its average level?
frontier_questions.gap_beginner: Nearly every study measures mTOR activity the way you would read a thermometer once: a single number, from a single moment, usually right after the cell was given a sudden jolt of nutrients. But real cells never get a sudden jolt. They get meals, exercise, sleep and waking — a rhythm. If what matters is the rhythm rather than the average, then the standard measurement is not just imprecise. It is answering a different question from the one being asked.

frontier_questions.title: Is mTOR signalling decided by where the complex is active, rather than by how much of it is active?
frontier_questions.gap_beginner: The lysosome is normally described as mTOR's parking space. Newer structural work describes it more like a workbench: what the enzyme can reach depends on how it is docked. If that is right, two cells with the same amount of activity can be doing completely different jobs — and grinding them up to measure the total would hide exactly that.

frontier_questions.title: Does the timing of mTOR inhibition have to match the body's own pulses — feeding, exercise, sleep?
frontier_questions.gap_beginner: Giving the drug once a week instead of daily is usually explained as a way to lower the dose and avoid side effects. But if the pathway cares about rhythm, the question is not how often you give it — it is whether the gaps in the drug line up with the moments the body actually needs the pathway on, like after a meal or after exercise. Nobody has tested that alignment.

frontier_questions.title: Is mTORC1 one pathway or several separable outputs — and which of them carries ageing?
frontier_questions.gap_beginner: Most of the argument is about how hard to press the brake, and recently about which of the two brakes to press. Hardly anyone asks which of the things the brake controls actually needs slowing. And those things do come apart: in muscle, fixing one downstream branch rescues the problem while removing another does nothing.

frontier_questions.title: Which human ageing phenotypes are causally reversible by mTOR modulation — and is it the same mechanism in each tissue?
frontier_questions.gap_beginner: Asking whether a drug makes people live longer cannot be answered in any reasonable amount of time, and aiming at it has crowded out better questions. Ageing is not one thing: the immune system, muscle, metabolism and the brain each age in their own way, and a drug might reach some of them and miss others entirely.

focus_table_intro: The foundational and most closely related studies behind the “pattern over time, not just average level” question above, ranked by scientific significance rather than publication date:

focus_studies.title: Tuberous sclerosis complex gene products, Tuberin and Hamartin, control mTOR signaling by acting as a GTPase-activating protein complex toward Rheb
focus_studies.why: Founding paper — first to show TSC1/TSC2 acting as the GAP complex for Rheb, the discovery the whole TSC→mTORC1 axis rests on.

focus_studies.title: Rheb GTPase is a direct target of TSC2 GAP activity and regulates mTOR signaling
focus_studies.why: Companion founding paper, published independently and simultaneously with Tee et al. 2003 — same weight, same discovery.

focus_studies.title: TSC2 is phosphorylated and inhibited by Akt and suppresses mTOR signalling
focus_studies.why: Established the Akt→TSC2→mTOR link — the exact “known regulatory input” Joshi 2024 shows is bypassed during interphase.

focus_studies.title: TBC1D7 is a third subunit of the TSC1-TSC2 complex upstream of mTORC1
focus_studies.why: Completed the parts list of the TSC complex whose GAP activity Joshi 2024 studies across the cell cycle.

focus_studies.title: Spatial control of the TSC complex integrates insulin and nutrient regulation of mTORC1 at the lysosome
focus_studies.why: Closest mechanistic precedent to the “timing, not just level” question — shows TSC complex localization, not just abundance, gates mTORC1.

focus_studies.title: Lysosomal positioning coordinates cellular nutrient responses
focus_studies.why: The spatial counterpart to Menétrey 2014, one storey up: with nutrients available lysosomes move out to the cell periphery and mTORC1 is active there; starvation pulls them into a cluster around the nucleus, output falls and autophagy is released. Where the compartment sits, not how much of it there is, carries the signal — and it sets the rate of autophagy directly.

focus_studies.title: Molecular logic of mTORC1 signalling as a metabolic rheostat
focus_studies.why: Conceptual framework from Joshi 2024's own senior author — mTORC1 as a graded rheostat rather than an on/off switch.

focus_studies.title: mTORC1 Couples Nucleotide Synthesis to Nucleotide Demand Resulting in a Targetable Metabolic Vulnerability
focus_studies.why: Same lab's translational angle — TSC-mutant cells' nucleotide synthesis as a druggable weak point.

focus_studies.title: mTORC1 activity oscillates throughout the cell cycle, promoting mitotic entry and differentially influencing autophagy induction
focus_studies.why: The paper that sparked this focus — mTORC1 activity is lowest in mitosis/G1 and highest in S/G2, and this timing, not just average level, shapes autophagy sensitivity.

focus_studies.title: AIMTOR, a BRET biosensor for live imaging, reveals subcellular mTOR signaling and dysfunctions
focus_studies.why: The enabling technology behind the question. AIMTOR reads mTOR activity live in single cells and separately in the cytosol, at the lysosome, in the nucleus and near mitochondria — which is what turns a pulsatile or oscillatory hypothesis from something arguable into something measurable. It came five years after TORCAR (ZHO2015), the first live mTORC1 reporter, and adds compartment-specific versions in a bioluminescence format.

focus_studies.title: Inferring feedback regulation from static snapshots of a single signal
focus_studies.why: A method for reading a signal’s change over time out of still images — and it finds AKT feedback that exists only in a narrow window at G1/S, which the authors attribute to mTORC1/S6K1→IRS1 while stating their data do not establish that edge uniquely.

focus_studies.title: Mathematical modeling of dietary timing- and protein quality-responsive liver circadian clock and its function on ribosome biogenesis
focus_studies.why: Treats mTORC1 as a rhythm set by the timing and quality of amino acid intake rather than a fixed level, and asks what the shape of that rhythm does to ribosome biogenesis. A prediction, not a measurement — the model is in silico.

focus_studies.title: Fluorescent protein ticker tape (FPTT): Multiplexed recording of transcriptional dynamics in living cells and in vivo
focus_studies.why: A new multiplexed live-cell biosensor platform that, built and validated independently of JOS2024, directly visualized mTOR activity oscillating across the cell cycle — orthogonal confirmation that the pattern of mTOR signaling over time is a real, reproducible phenomenon rather than an artifact of one assay.

focus_studies.title: Alternative rapamycin treatment regimens mitigate the impact of rapamycin on glucose homeostasis and the immune system
focus_studies.why: One of two studies in this corpus that hold the compound constant and vary only when it is given (the other, OKA2013, varies the time of day): weekly or every-fifth-day rapamycin spared glucose tolerance, beta-cell function and the immune system that daily dosing impaired, while still inhibiting mTORC1. Read the scope honestly — this is organismal pharmacology rather than cell-level signalling, and it measured side effects, not benefit. It belongs here because it is the same claim in a different register: the pattern, not the average, decided the outcome.

focus_studies.title: Dynamic Visualization of mTORC1 Activity in Living Cells
focus_studies.why: The first genetically encoded reporter of mTORC1 activity: a FRET sensor that shows mTORC1 changing in living cells, in real time and compartment by compartment. It found activity in the nucleus and at the plasma membrane as well as at the lysosome, with different signals lighting up different places. Without a live reader, the question of whether the pattern matters could not be asked of mTORC1 at all.

focus_studies.title: Temporal coding of insulin action through multiplexing of the AKT pathway
focus_studies.why: The cleanest cell-level proof that timing carries information in this pathway: a pulse of insulin and a sustained dose became transient and sustained AKT signals, and S6K answered only the transient one. It sits one step upstream of mTORC1 and uses a rat liver cell line, so it is not mTORC1's own rhythm. What it shows is the principle the question rests on: same pathway, same molecules, and the shape of the signal decides which output responds.

focus_studies.title: Dietary protein governs the role of insulin signaling in the postprandial regulation of hepatic mTORC1
focus_studies.why: A direct look at how mTORC1 switches with the feeding cycle in a living animal: in mouse liver, the rise after a meal needs dietary protein, and insulin's AKT-TSC2 route explains the insulin response but not the feeding response. It is a mouse liver study with fasting versus fed states, not a continuous time course, so it shows which signals set the on/off pattern rather than the rhythm itself.

on_the_horizon_intro: Not yet part of the graded corpus above — because they are either still running or have not been peer-reviewed — but directly relevant, found via ClinicalTrials.gov and bioRxiv:

on_the_horizon.title: RESTOR — Rapamycin and Everolimus Study Towards Older Rejuvenation
on_the_horizon.why: The most direct human test of this question so far: it first measures mTOR activity in young adults as a “youthful” target, then compares daily vs. intermittent dosing against placebo in older adults over 6 months, tracking S6/S6K and Akt phosphorylation in blood, muscle and fat — pattern vs. level, not just dose vs. no dose.
on_the_horizon.expected: Primary completion Jul 2028; no results posted yet

on_the_horizon.title: RAP PAC — Safer mTOR Inhibition for Human Geroprotection
on_the_horizon.why: Weekly dosing with blood drawn out to 168 hours post-dose — a real time-course of mTOR inhibition in older adults, rather than a single before/after measurement.
on_the_horizon.expected: Primary completion Mar 2027; study completion Dec 2028; no results posted yet

on_the_horizon.title: Characterization of mTOR Inhibitor Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics in Older Adults
on_the_horizon.why: Hourly blood draws after dosing track S6K activity as a curve rather than a point, alongside a senescence marker (SASP index) — the PK/PD groundwork this frontier question needs before intermittent regimens can be tested properly.
on_the_horizon.expected: Primary completion Sep 2027; study completion Nov 2027; no results posted yet

on_the_horizon.title: TSC1 phosphorylation by lysosomal mTORC1 establishes a minimal autoregulatory feedback loop
on_the_horizon.why: Shows mTORC1 phosphorylating TSC1, part of its own inhibitory brake — a candidate mechanism for how a self-limiting pulse of activity could arise inside a cell, rather than being imposed only by external nutrient swings.
on_the_horizon.expected: Data already public; journal version not found as of 30 Sep 2026

on_the_horizon.title: mTORC1 supports progression toward activation competence in quiescent adult neural stem cells
on_the_horizon.why: A different cell type — adult neural stem cells — where the timing of mTORC1 activity during a quiescence phase, not just whether it is on, sets the tempo of a cell-fate decision. Evidence that this isn't a phenomenon specific to cycling cancer cell lines.
on_the_horizon.expected: Data already public; journal version not found as of 30 Sep 2026

on_the_horizon.title: The mTOR pathway drives daily physiology
on_the_horizon.why: Shows the circadian clock protein PERIOD2 binds mTORC1 directly, and that acutely blocking mTOR abolishes most daily rhythms in mouse liver and forebrain physiology without stopping the core clock itself — direct evidence that mTOR acts as a clock-output arm pacing physiology across the day, not just a nutrient-responsive switch.
on_the_horizon.model: Mouse and zebrafish; also cells, plant, fungus
on_the_horizon.expected: Data already public; journal version not found as of 30 Sep 2026

on_the_horizon.title: Understanding the Effects of Obesity on Autophagic and mTORC1 Signalling Following Resistance Exercise and Protein Ingestion in Skeletal Muscle
on_the_horizon.why: Tracks mTORC1-lysosomal translocation and autophagic flux at multiple timepoints before and after a single bout of resistance exercise plus protein feeding, comparing lean vs. obese adults — a direct human time-course of mTORC1 activation kinetics, not a single before/after snapshot, tied explicitly to an autophagy endpoint.
on_the_horizon.expected: Primary completion Dec 2026; study completion Dec 2027; no results posted yet

labs_intro: Research groups whose work bears most directly on the question above, grouped by how they get at it. Each one links to the lab's own page; photos link to the lab head's profile in the Atlas.

labs.group: Measuring how mTOR activity changes over time, and what that timing does

items.why: Showed that mTORC1 activity rises and falls through the cell cycle, and that cells low in mTORC1 during G1 are pushed into autophagy more easily. This is the study the whole focus grew out of.
Studies how mTORC1 sets a target size for cells, and built a method for reading how a signal changes over time out of fixed snapshots.
Films mTORC1–TFEB, AMPK and AKT signalling in single living cells and showed that mTORC1 output adjusts continuously as nutrients change.
Showed in single yeast cells that TORC1 activity oscillates with the cell cycle even when nothing outside the cell changes, a yeast counterpart to the Valvezan result.
Found that mTOR briefly switches off the APC/C as a cell starts to divide, creating a short pulse of glycolysis the cell needs to get going.

Showed that different time courses of insulin are read out by different branches of the AKT pathway, S6K among them: an early, direct demonstration that the shape of a signal carries information, not just its level.
A 2026 preprint from the lab reports that mTORC1 sets the tempo at which dormant neural stem cells in the adult zebrafish brain move toward activation.

items.institution: Massachusetts General Hospital & Harvard Stem Cell Institute
items.why: Imaged mTORC1 activity in leukaemia cells inside live mice and found that inhibiting mTORC1 at one particular moment during chemotherapy kills more cancer cells.

labs.group: Tools for watching mTOR activity live

items.why: Built TORCAR, a FRET biosensor that shows mTORC1 activity in living cells as it happens, including in separate parts of the cell.

items.institution: IGF (CNRS/INSERM) and DMEM (INRAE), University of Montpellier
items.why: Co-developed AIMTOR, a BRET biosensor that reads mTOR activity live in single cells and in compartments such as the lysosome and the nucleus.
Filmed mTORC1 moving to lysosomes within two minutes of adding amino acids, before its targets are phosphorylated.

labs.group: Rhythm and dosing in the whole organism

items.why: Found that mTOR activity in the liver follows a daily rhythm set by feeding, and compares calorie restriction with cycles of fasting and refeeding.
Models liver mTORC1 as a rhythm set by when and what an animal eats, and asks what that rhythm does to ribosome production.
Showed that rapamycin given once every five days still extends mouse lifespan with fewer side effects, so the dosing schedule matters, not just the dose.

items.institution: UCL Institute of Healthy Ageing (and MPI for Biology of Ageing, Cologne, emerita)
items.why: Showed that a brief course of rapamycin in early adulthood gives lasting protection against ageing, and that intermittent rapamycin feeding keeps the lifespan benefit.
